hypothesis: An adversary who compromised Windows hosts in this network stole credentials from them (MITRE ATT&CK tactic: Credential Access).

frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network is stealing credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: Observable evidence such as LSASS process memory access (e.g., via Mimikatz or procdump), suspicious access to SAM/SECURITY registry hives, NTDS.dit extraction, credential dumping tool execution, or anomalous authentication events indicating credential theft.
frame.what_would_refute: Absence of credential dumping tool execution, no unauthorized access to LSASS or credential stores, no suspicious registry hive or NTDS.dit access, and no anomalous authentication events consistent with stolen credentials.

verdict.rationale: 5 in-scope incident(s) of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium): I02 T1003.001 (F01, F05, F13, F37, F39), I03 T1056.002 (F12), I06 T1552 (F02, F14, F33, F38), I07 T1552.001 (F32, F61, F62, F64), I08 T1552.004 (F31, F59)
verdict.rule: Confirmed if >=1 in-scope incident of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium); Inconclusive if only suspicious incidents or coverage gaps; Refuted if full coverage and no malicious/suspicious finding

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: lsass.exe created C:\Windows\debug\PASSWD.LOG on scranton (CreationUtcTime 2020-03-12, likely pre-existing); no new distinct dump beyond the anchored LSASS access.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: PowerShell.exe on scranton accessed lsass.exe with 0x1FFFFF/0x1f3fff and an UNKNOWN call-trace module; wsmprovhost.exe on nashua accessed lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: No reg save/esentutl/vssadmin, no SAM/SECURITY hive file writes; only benign Prefetch files matched.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No ntdsutil/vssadmin/diskshadow/ntds.dit activity or ntds file writes.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: No dedicated LSA-secrets tooling, but LSASS memory was accessed (LSA secrets live in LSASS).

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: No 4663 access to Cache/SECURITY objects and no cache/DCC2/mscache script blocks.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: No DCSync/lsadump script blocks and no DRSUAPI dce_rpc in zeek.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: No packet-sniffing tooling or promiscuous-mode capture was found on any host. The only capture activity is the legitimate Azure NetworkWatcherAgent invoking netsh trace (parent NetworkWatcherAgent.exe, part of the Azure Guest Agent lifecycle) on scranton.dmevals.local. Searches for windump/tcpdump/wireshark/dumpcap/pktmon/rawcap/Npcap in sysmon event.code:1 and security 4688 returned 0 hits, no pcap driver image-load (event.code:6) was seen, and no PowerShell 4104 script block referenced sniffing/capture/pcap/promiscuous. Zeek weird records are benign sensor-side parsing artifacts (ip_hdr_len_zero, truncated_IP, unknown_dce_rpc_auth_type) in a non-overlapping time window. The genuine malicious activity in the window (PsExec with plaintext credentials, python.exe payload, sdelete) is credential access/lateral movement, not network sniffing.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: PowerShell (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF on scranton, and pbeesly's session harvested credential-bearing files and staged them for exfiltration.

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: All Keyboard/keylog registry writes are benign Windows keyboard-layout and device-enumeration writes by System/winlogon/LogonUI; no keylogger driver, hook, or keyboard-object access found.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: pbeesly defined and invoked Invoke-ScreenCapture, a PowerShell loop using System.Windows.Forms CopyFromScreen to capture the full screen to .bmp files every 300s on scranton.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No inetpub/aspx/ashx writes, no PowerShell web-content writes, and no HTTP POST in the zeek window; only WebDAV exfiltration staging was seen.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: No lsass-related messages in windows.other and no injected/hooked credential-provider DLLs; only the single full-access PowerShell LSASS open, already reported under T1056.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: Zero 4625 failed logons and no repeated authentication failures in any dataset; the only 4776 is a success (Status 0x0). No brute-force pattern.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: No failed logons (4625=0, 4771=0); runas/net use hits are benign Windows binaries (svchost, conhost, WmiPrvSE). No guessing.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: No hashcat/john/crack tooling and no cracking output files; lsass accesses are from svchost/Azure agents and one 0x1000 handle from powershell, not memory-read dumping.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: 4648 explicit-credential logons are all one account (pbeesly) reused across scranton/nashua via PSEXESVC, i.e. lateral movement, not many accounts sprayed against one host; no 4625/4771 failures.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No credential-list file arguments (only logman.exe with .txt); PowerShell credential use is hardcoded single secrets (saribas, cozy/MyCozyPassw0rd!), not stuffing of stolen credential pairs.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA/smartcard interception artifacts. Registry 'Credential'/'Smartcard' hits are benign Windows service registration (CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc, SCardSvr.dll MuiCache) and CredentialGuard\Enabled=0x0 set by lsass.exe. 4648 explicit-credential logons are pbeesly credentials used by PSEXESVC.exe/svchost.exe and normal winlogon/wininit/taskhostw infrastructure accounts. PowerShell 4104 references a hardcoded credential for WebDAV exfiltration, not MFA token interception. Activity is credential use/theft, not T1111.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: No forced-authentication activity found. All SMB (445/139) connections are internal System-process traffic to internal hosts (10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.6, IPv6 loopback); share access is machine-account SYSVOL/IPC$ domain activity; no UNC/WebDAV file writes; the only NTLM event is a benign per-boot LsaSrv 6038 warning. PowerShell hits are collection/steganography, not coercion.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: No exploitation of a vulnerability for credential access was observed. All 326 lsass process-access events are svchost.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1000 via lsm.dll/RPCRT4 (normal LSA RPC), the only WebDAV payload fetch (/webdav/python.exe) returned HTTP 401 Unauthorized, and the PowerShell/Kerberos activity reflects post-exploitation tradecraft and routine ticket requests rather than exploit-driven credential theft.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: No process read, copied or archived a browser cookie/session database. The only cookie/browser-profile file events are MicrosoftEdge.exe writing its own profile files and svchost.exe creating a system INetCookies folder on scranton.dmevals.local — normal browser/OS behaviour. Sysmon event 10 against browser images and event 2 creation of Cookies/Login Data returned zero hits, and no PowerShell script block referenced cookie/sqlite extraction. The suspicious APT29-style PowerShell on scranton (screen capture, 7-Zip exfil to WebDAV) is unrelated to web session cookie theft.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: PyInstaller python.exe staged/executed via PSEXESVC on nashua, spawning powershell.exe.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: PowerShell credential-file harvesting on nashua (search for *pass*/*login*/*admin*/*vpn*, archive to working.zip), password-protected RAR staging, and accesschk.exe writing passwordsDB on scranton.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: All Password/Credential/Winlogon registry writes came from svchost/winlogon/lsass/services; no reg query/save/export and no adversary registry credential reads.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: Zero hits for ConsoleHost_history/PSReadLine in PowerShell, sysmon command lines and file paths.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: Get-PrivateKeys exported machine certificate private keys to C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx, confirmed by the sysmon file-creation event.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: SYSVOL/GptTmpl.inf/gpt.ini access was routine svchost.exe Group Policy client activity and normal zeek SMB policy retrieval; no Groups.xml/cpassword access.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: PowerShell.exe on scranton opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff (full access) at 03:05:16, corroborated by a 4663 object-access event by powershell.exe as pbeesly; wsmprovhost.exe on nashua opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: All browser credential-store checks (Login Data, logins.json, key4.db, signons.sqlite, Local State) returned zero hits in sysmon, security and powershell datasets.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: pbeesly on scranton ran Get-PrivateKeys (exported LocalMachine cert private keys with password 'saribas'), Get-Clipboard and a Get-Keystrokes keylogger from a SysinternalsSuite-hosted toolkit, alongside the LSASS full-access handle.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: All password-manager checks (keepass, 1password, lastpass, bitwarden) and Vault/Credential hive checks returned zero hits across all four datasets.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: LSASS was opened with full access (0x1FFFFF) by PowerShell.exe under user pbeesly on scranton, and Security 4663 confirms pbeesly/powershell.exe reading lsass.exe. This is credential theft from LSASS memory rather than authentication-process modification, so the T1556 family itself is not confirmed.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: No DC authentication tampering; LSASS access was dominated by legitimate system processes and no LSA/Security Packages registry modifications were found.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No password filter DLL file drops or Notification Packages/PasswordFilter registry writes; cryptdll/samlib loads are normal Microsoft DLLs.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: No 4739 events and no reversible-encryption command lines or messages.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No 4739 or 5136 events and no MFA/authentication-policy command lines.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No 5136 directory-service changes; dsregcmd.exe cryptdll load is normal Azure AD device registration.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No network provider DLL registration; observed registry writes were benign notification/LogonUI/WMI Autologger keys.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: No AiTM positioning: SMB traffic is normal domain GPO/IPC$ activity and PsExec lateral movement; no interception tooling or MITM host identified.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: No LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning or SMB relay: only 2 NBT-NS connections, no LLMNR, normal DNS rcodes, SMB sources limited to normal internal hosts.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: No ARP cache poisoning: only 3 distinct source MACs in Zeek with no duplication or conflicting L2 addresses.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP (67/68) traffic anywhere; the only anomaly is a brief, reverted Microsoft NDIS Capture service start-type toggle on scranton, which is low-confidence and not a rogue DHCP server.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: No stolen/forged Kerberos tickets: all 4769 tickets are AES256 (0x12), zeek kerberos shows only normal AS/TGS for pbeesly with aes256, and 5857/5858 events are WMI/RSOP noise from SYSTEM.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: No RC4 TGTs, no krbtgt/golden/Rubeus strings in PowerShell or process command lines; the only full-access LSASS reads are generic PowerShell credential access, not KRBTGT extraction.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: TGS requests target only machine accounts and krbtgt with AES256 encryption and Status 0x0; no RC4 service tickets or anomalous service-account sessions.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: All 28 TGS requests use AES256 (0x12), not RC4; no Kerberoast/Invoke-Kerberoast/GetUserSPNs strings found; 4648 logons are PsExec lateral movement, not roasting.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: Zeek kerberos shows pre-auth enforced (KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED then AES256 success) for pbeesly; no AS-REP/GetNPUsers/Rubeus strings found.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: No forged web credential artifacts. Cookie/token-related hits are benign (WebDAV DavSetCookie, UWP INetCookies, Microsoft module manifests). Logon-process stacking shows only Kerberos/Advapi/User32/NtLmSsp. The window's real activity is a credential-access/collection chain (PsExec with plaintext creds, WebDAV exfil, sdelete), not T1606.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: No cookie theft or forging. Only cookie-related events are a UWP INetCookies file create and standard davclnt.dll DavSetCookie WebDAV client calls; no cookie-forging tooling or scripts.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: No SAML token forging. No ADFS/token-signing service activity; PowerShell *SAML*/*certificate* hits are Microsoft module manifest strings. LSASS access is normal svchost 0x1000 LSA RPC, not token-signing material theft.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: No MFA request generation activity found. Zero failed logons (4625=0), no MFA/2FA/Authenticator/Duo/Okta/Push strings in PowerShell script blocks, and the only 7045 service installs are PsExec (PSEXESVC) and a Java support service - lateral movement artifacts, not MFA-fatigue tooling. Authentication events are successful explicit-credential logons (4648) to NASHUA over SMB.

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.reason: A PowerShell script (Get-PrivateKeys, from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) run by user pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local enumerated cert:\LocalMachine and exported every certificate's private key to a .pfx file (C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx) protected by the hardcoded password "saribas", with matching Sysmon file-create and SystemCertificates\MY registry writes by the same PowerShell PID 3876 — direct theft of authentication certificate private keys.

findings.title: LSASS memory accessed with full-access masks by PowerShell.exe on scranton and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:05:16, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) and 0x1f3fff, with a CallTrace ending in an UNKNOWN module (UNKNOWN(000001996D28200D)) rather than a signed system DLL — the classic signature of an in-memory LSASS dump. The same access mask 0x1f3fff against lsass.exe was used by wsmprovhost.exe (WinRM remote PowerShell) on nashua.dmevals.local at 03:09:29. This occurred in the middle of a post-exploitation PowerShell toolkit run by user pbeesly on scranton (Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence, Get-PrivateKeys, Invoke-ScreenCapture, Get-Keystrokes, Invoke-Exfil loaded from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1). The Windows security log independently records pbeesly's powershell.exe accessing \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe at 03:05:16. The 0x1000 accesses by svchost.exe and the 0x1fffff accesses by wininit.exe/csrss.exe at 03:19:09 are normal system behaviour (boot-time), but the PowerShell/wsmprovhost accesses with read-memory masks are not.

findings.title: PowerShell screen-capture function (Invoke-ScreenCapture) run by pbeesly on scranton
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:05:53 UTC on scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly (S-1-5-21-1830255721-3727074217-2423397540-1107) defined and then invoked a PowerShell function 'Invoke-ScreenCapture' (script block path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1). One second later sysmon recorded the resulting file creation C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx by powershell.exe, confirming the export actually ran. incidents.title: lsass.exe writing C:\Windows\debug\PASSWD.LOG on scranton
incidents.rationale: F65 documents a Sysmon file-create event showing lsass.exe (PID 748) creating C:\Windows\debug\PASSWD.LOG on scranton.dmevals.local, with a CreationUtcTime of 2020-03-12 suggesting a pre-existing file re-touched rather than a fresh dump — a credential-named artifact on the compromised host, best fitting OS Credential Dumping (T1003) at low confidence.

incidents.title: LSASS memory accessed with full-access masks by PowerShell on scranton and wsmprovhost on nashua
incidents.rationale: All five findings describe the same action: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, user pbeesly) on scranton.dmevals.local opening lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff/0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) with an UNKNOWN-module CallTrace, corroborated by the 4663 object-access event on \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe, plus the same 0x1f3fff mask used by wsmprovhost.exe on nashua.dmevals.local. F05 and F39 explicitly note no separate LSA-secrets or auth-process modification artifact exists, so the best-fitting in-scope technique is LSASS memory dumping (T1003.001).

incidents.title: PowerShell screen-capture function (Invoke-ScreenCapture) run by pbeesly on scranton
incidents.rationale: F12 documents pbeesly defining and invoking Invoke-ScreenCapture on scranton.dmevals.local, a background job using System.Windows.Forms/System.Drawing CopyFromScreen to capture the screen — GUI input capture, matching T1056.002.

incidents.title: PowerShell script blocks are credential/file collection, not forced authentication
incidents.rationale: F27 documents that the 4104 script blocks on scranton.dmevals.local under pbeesly are recursive enumeration of credential-named user files compressed to $env:APPDATA\Draft.Zip and a System.Drawing bitmap steganography loader (monkey.png) — collection/credential-access behavior with no UNC/WebDAV coercion or outbound authentication trigger, so it is not T1187.

incidents.title: APT29-style PowerShell screen capture and exfil present but unrelated to cookie theft
incidents.rationale: F30 documents the same pbeesly PowerShell tooling on scranton.dmevals.local (Invoke-ScreenCapture, Invoke-Exfil with 7-Zip password 'lolol' and WebDAV copy to \\192.168.0.4\webdav) but explicitly notes it does not touch browser cookie stores, so it is not T1539 activity.

incidents.title: Post-exploitation PowerShell credential toolkit run by pbeesly on scranton
incidents.rationale: These findings all describe the same pbeesly PowerShell session on scranton.dmevals.local loading a multi-function toolkit from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite (psversion.ps1/readme.ps1): Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence, Get-PrivateKeys, Invoke-ScreenCapture, Get-Keystrokes, Get-Clipboard, credential-file harvesting, Invoke-Exfil and Invoke-BeachCleanup, plus hidden encoded PowerShell, a Javasoft registry Invoke-Expression one-liner, hostui.exe elevation and a monkey.png steganographic loader. The unifying action is harvesting unsecured credentials and credential-bearing files from the host, best fitting T1552.

incidents.title: Hardcoded credentials in attacker PowerShell tooling and explicit-credential logons to NASHUA
incidents.rationale: These findings all concern credentials found in files and attacker tooling: Invoke-Exfil embedding plaintext credentials ($UserName 'cozy', $Password 'MyCozyPassw0rd!') and mapping \\192.168.0.4\webdav, pbeesly's explicit-credential logons to NASHUA, the nashua PowerShell harvesting of *pass*/*login*/*admin*/*vpn* files into working.zip, the password-protected RAR archive (-hpfGzq5yKw) with sdelete wiping, and accesschk.exe writing passwordsDB on scranton. The unifying action is credentials in files, matching T1552.001.

incidents.title: Get-PrivateKeys exported machine certificate private keys to .pfx on scranton
incidents.rationale: F31 and F59 describe the same action: pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local running Get-PrivateKeys (from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1), which enumerates cert:\LocalMachine and calls Export-PfxCertificate for every certificate with a Thumbprint, writing private keys to $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\<random>.pfx protected by hardcoded password 'saribas', with the .pfx file creation and certificate registry blob events corroborating it. This is private-key theft, matching T1552.004.

incidents.title: No DHCP spoofing; NDIS Capture service toggle is a brief reverted change
incidents.rationale: F49 documents that no DHCP traffic (UDP 67/68) exists in any dataset; the only anomaly is a 4-second toggle of the Microsoft NDIS Capture service start type on scranton.dmevals.local, consistent with a packet-capture driver being briefly enabled rather than a rogue DHCP server, and the xDNSServerAddress script blocks on newyork are legitimate DSC. Not T1557.003.

incidents.title: PsExec lateral movement with plaintext credentials and python.exe payload on nashua
incidents.rationale: These findings describe the same activity: pbeesly using PsExec64.exe with plaintext credentials (-u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by) to install PSEXESVC and launch C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on \\NASHUA, the 4648 explicit-credential logons being PsExec-driven reuse of one account (not spraying, not MFA interception), and the PyInstaller python.exe executing as a child of PSEXESVC.exe. This is remote service execution/lateral movement, not credential access, so it is out-of-scope (T1021).
